'''Keith Usherwood Ingold''' {{Post-nominals|country=CAN|OC|FRS|FRSC|FRSE}} (31 May 1929 – 8 September 2023) was a British-Canadian chemist.

==Life and career==
Keith Usherwood Ingold was born to [[Christopher Kelk Ingold|Sir Christopher Ingold]] and [[Hilda Ingold|Dr. Hilda Usherwood]], and studied for a [[Bachelor of Science|BSc]] in Chemistry at the [[University of London]], completing his degree in 1949. He continued his higher education with a [[Doctor of Philosophy|PhD]] in chemistry at [[University of Oxford|Oxford University]], which he completed in 1951. Soon after graduation he moved to Canada to begin work with the [[National Research Council (Canada)|National Research Council]], followed by two years of post-doctoral research at the [[University of British Columbia]].<ref name="msu">{{cite web|url=http://www.chemistry.msu.edu/Lectureships/lectures.asp?series=MTR&Year=2000|title=MSU Chemistry – Max T Rogers Lectureship|accessdate=2008-11-15|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20100714093902/http://www2.chemistry.msu.edu/Lectureships/lectures.asp?series=MTR&Year=2000|archive-date=14 July 2010|url-status=dead}}</ref> He returned to work for the NRC in 1955 as a research officer, followed by a promotion to head of the Free Radical Chemistry Section. He was awarded the 1968 Petroleum Chemistry Award, the 1988 Linus Pauling Award, and both the [[Davy Medal]] and [[Royal Medal]] of the [[Royal Society]], the latter for "elucidating the mechanism of reactions involving free radicals".<ref>{{cite web|url=https://royalsociety.org/people/keith-ingold-11678/|accessdate=2023-10-08 |title=Keith Ingold }}</ref> In 1995 he was made an officer of the [[Order of Canada]].<ref>{{OCC|3283}}</ref> He has received honorary degrees from the universities of [[University of Guelph|Guelph]], [[Mount Allison University|Mount Allison]], [[University of St Andrews|St Andrews]], [[Carleton University|Carleton]], [[McMaster University|McMaster]] and [[Dalhousie University|Dalhousie]].<ref name="msu"/>

In his later career, Ingold's work focused on radical-trapping [[antioxidant]]s, [[vitamin E]] in particular, and their effect on aging<ref name=MacKay/> and on preventing such age-related diseases as [[cancer]].

Ingold died in Ottawa, Ontario on 8 September 2023, at the age of 94.<ref name=MacKay>{{cite web|title=Organic chemist explored connection between free radicals and aging|url=https://www.theglobeandmail.com/canada/article-organic-chemist-explored-connection-between-free-radicals-and-aging/|publisher=The Globe and Mail|url-access = limited|date=5 October 2023|last=Mackay|first=Susan Ferrer|access-date=8 October 2023}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |url=https://www.legacy.com/ca/obituaries/theglobeandmail/name/keith-ingold-obituary?id=53113658 |title=Keith Usherwood Ingold |work=The Globe & Mail |via=Legacy.com |access-date=September 16, 2023}}</ref>
